packet.headline_seed: It was 'love at first sight' with their adopted baby. Then they were told he may have been trafficked
packet.description_seed: When they adopted Marcus, David and Ally's dream of having a child was complete - but now they could lose him.

what: It was 'love at first sight' with their adopted baby. Then they were told he may have been trafficked

clean_source_blocks.text: When they adopted Marcus, David and Ally's dream of having a child was complete - but now they could lose him.

Many of the babies have by now spent most of their lives in Singapore (Stock image of a family with toddler) When David and Ally first saw Marcus, they knew he was destined to be their son. "For me it was love at first sight," said David. Their long adoption journey had come to an end. Months later, the baby from Indonesia was in their arms and the family was ready to start their life together. But now, years later, they face the possibility of losing Marcus because he is believed to have been trafficked into Singapore.

He is one of at least 20 babies alleged to have been illegally bought in Indonesia for adoption in Singapore in recent years. Nearly two dozen people have been arrested for alleged human trafficking last year and are now on trial in West Java. This means authorities may have to decide if Marcus and other children, who would by now have spent most of their lives in Singapore, should stay with their adoptive parents or return to their biological parents in Indonesia. Both countries have yet to state what will happen to the children. For David and Ally, these last few months have been agonising. The high-profile case has highlighted the enduring problem of child trafficking in Indonesia, fuelled by parents who sell their children.

It has also raised questions over how Singapore - known for its tight controls and meticulous checks - failed to detect the alleged trafficking and even approved some of the adoptions. David and Ally agreed to share their story with the BBC on condition we use pseudonyms, as they fear jeopardising their chance to keep Marcus. "The anxiety is always there, at the back of our minds," said David. "There's always the thought that Marcus might be taken away." David and Ally had always wanted children but after Ally went through several painful miscarriages, they decided to adopt. But they faced a long wait for a Singaporean child - with one adoption agency giving them a queue number of 142.

original_article.research:
[Lähde: BBC World]
Many of the babies have by now spent most of their lives in Singapore (Stock image of a family with toddler)

When David and Ally first saw Marcus, they knew he was destined to be their son.

"For me it was love at first sight," said David. Their long adoption journey had come to an end. Months later, the baby from Indonesia was in their arms and the family was ready to start their life together.

But now, years later, they face the possibility of losing Marcus because he is believed to have been trafficked into Singapore.

He is one of at least 20 babies alleged to have been illegally bought in Indonesia for adoption in Singapore in recent years. Nearly two dozen people have been arrested for alleged human trafficking last year and are now on trial in West Java.

This means authorities may have to decide if Marcus and other children, who would by now have spent most of their lives in Singapore, should stay with their adoptive parents or return to their biological parents in Indonesia.

Both countries have yet to state what will happen to the children. For David and Ally, these last few months have been agonising.

The high-profile case has highlighted the enduring problem of child trafficking in Indonesia, fuelled by parents who sell their children.

It has also raised questions over how Singapore - known for its tight controls and meticulous checks - failed to detect the alleged trafficking and even approved some of the adoptions.

David and Ally agreed to share their story with the BBC on condition we use pseudonyms, as they fear jeopardising their chance to keep Marcus.

"The anxiety is always there, at the back of our minds," said David.

"There's always the thought that Marcus might be taken away."

David and Ally had always wanted children but after Ally went through several painful miscarriages, they decided to adopt.

But they faced a long wait for a Singaporean child - with one adoption agency giving them a queue number of 142.

So they did what many Singaporeans in this situation do, and looked overseas. An estimated two-thirds of the children adopted in Singapore every year were born elsewhere, usually in neighbouring countries.

David and Ally chose a local agency that specialised in arranging adoptions of Indonesian babies.

Weeks later, they were peering at a tiny infant held up to the camera, in a video call arranged by the agency.

"What was so special about him that caught our attention? He's very smart ! He smiled at us," recalled David.

payload.title: Adoptioperhe pelkää menettävänsä lapsen ihmiskauppaepäilyn vuoksi
payload.summary: Singaporessa asuva adoptioperhe sai vuosia lapsen adoptoimisen jälkeen kuulla, että heidän poikansa saattaa olla yksi Indonesiasta laittomasti adoptoiduista vauvoista.
payload.content:
David ja Ally luulivat pitkän adoptiomatkansa päättyneen, kun Indonesiasta tullut Marcus-vauva pääsi heidän syliinsä Singaporessa. Vuosia myöhemmin perhe elää epävarmuudessa, sillä viranomaiset selvittävät, voiko Marcus olla yksi vauvoista, joiden epäillään joutuneen ihmiskaupan kohteiksi.

## Epäilty vauvavälitys koskee ainakin 20 lasta

Marcus on yksi ainakin 20 vauvasta, joiden väitetään tulleen ostetuiksi laittomasti Indonesiassa ja adoptoiduiksi Singaporeen viime vuosina. Tapaukseen liittyen lähes kaksikymmentä ihmistä on pidätetty epäillystä ihmiskaupasta, ja he ovat parhaillaan oikeudenkäynnissä Länsi-Jaavalla.

Viranomaisten ratkaistavaksi voi nousta vaikea kysymys: pitäisikö Marcus ja muut lapset jättää adoptiovanhemmilleen Singaporeen vai palauttaa biologisille vanhemmilleen Indonesiaan. Monet lapsista ovat ehtineet viettää suurimman osan elämästään Singaporessa. Kumpikaan maa ei ole vielä kertonut, mitä lapsille aiotaan tehdä.

David ja Ally esiintyvät jutussa peitenimillä, koska he pelkäävät vaarantavansa mahdollisuutensa pitää Marcus luonaan. David kuvasi ensikohtaamista lapseen rakkaudeksi ensi silmäyksellä. Nyt perheen arkea varjostaa hänen mukaansa jatkuva ajatus siitä, että Marcus saatetaan ottaa pois.

## Tapaus herättää kysymyksiä valvonnasta

Tapaus on nostanut esiin Indonesian pitkäaikaisen lapsikauppaongelman. Lähdetietojen mukaan ilmiötä ylläpitävät myös tilanteet, joissa vanhemmat myyvät lapsiaan.

Samalla huomio on kohdistunut Singaporeen, joka tunnetaan tiukoista tarkastuksistaan ja huolellisesta valvonnastaan. Avoimeksi on jäänyt, miten väitetty ihmiskauppa jäi havaitsematta ja miten osa adoptioista hyväksyttiin järjestelmässä, jonka pitäisi seuloa tällaiset riskit.

Davidin ja Allyn tie adoptioon alkoi, kun he olivat pitkään toivoneet lasta. Ally oli kokenut useita raskaita keskenmenoja, minkä jälkeen pariskunta päätti adoptoida. Singaporen sisäinen adoptio olisi kuitenkin merkinnyt pitkää odotusta: eräs adoptiotoimisto antoi heille jononumeroksi 142.

Nyt perhe odottaa viranomaisten ratkaisuja tilanteessa, jossa oikeudenkäynti Indonesiassa jatkuu ja lasten tulevaisuus on yhä auki. Davidin mukaan ahdistus on jatkuvasti taustalla, koska perhe ei tiedä, saako Marcus jäädä kotiinsa Singaporeen.
summary_bullets: Singaporessa asuva adoptioperhe pelkää menettävänsä Indonesiasta adoptoidun Marcus-pojan.
Marcus saattaa olla yksi ainakin 20 vauvasta, joiden väitetään joutuneen laittoman adoptiovälityksen kohteiksi.
Lähes kaksikymmentä ihmistä on pidätetty epäillystä ihmiskaupasta, ja tapausta käsitellään oikeudessa Länsi-Jaavalla.
payload.journalist_note: Artikkeli perustuu annetun paketin tietoihin. Nimet David, Ally ja Marcus ovat lähdeaineiston mukaan peitenimiä; maiden viranomaiset eivät ole vielä kertoneet lasten kohtalosta.
